candidates.title: AceiiLab’s Robotic Tennis Ball Machine Has Cameras, Wheels, And Fits In Your Car’s Trunk
candidates.full_text:
In 1970, an inventor in Princeton, New Jersey, put a vacuum-cleaner motor to an unlikely new use: launching tennis balls. Bob McClure’s “Little Prince” became the starting point for Prince’s tennis-equipment business, and the basic ball machine format stayed remarkably familiar for decades afterward. You park a box on the baseline, it feeds balls from one spot, and you supply the imagination. More than half a century later, solo practice poses a different design question: how do you move beyond feeding balls to create more of the rhythm and responsiveness of a hitting partner? AceiiLab’s A1, a moving AI tennis robot, answers that question with wheels, cameras, and a lot of repositioning.

First introduced on Kickstarter in 2025 under the name Aceii One, the AceiiLab A1 approaches that question through movement. Its wheeled base can reposition for subsequent feeds, bringing changing angles and footwork into a solo session. Founder Liu Liqian previously built robots at DJI and KUKA, and that robotics background shows in how much of the product revolves around motion. For players fitting tennis around work, family, and someone else’s calendar, the appeal is practical: training on their own schedule, with more of the rhythm of playing across from someone. Launch speed tops out at a brisk 80 mph, though the real workout comes from what its movement asks the player to do next.

In tennis, the shot is only part of the exchange. You adjust your feet, recover your position, read the other side of the court, and prepare again. Changing pace and placement is one part of that practice, and changing where the next feed originates adds another spatial variable. The A1 makes that variable central to its design, giving solo players more to respond to than a stream of balls arriving from one stationary source. It moves at up to 13.1 feet per second (about 4 meters per second), which is quick enough that standing still to admire your last shot stops being an option.

AceiiLab pairs 4K binocular vision, which judges depth the way your eyes do, with a wheeled base that tracks the player and ball and repositions for each feed. Baseline, sideline, and service-line modes offer different setups, with the sideline and service-line options echoing how coaches feed beginners from the same side of the net. Adjustable timing, from 0.5 to 15 seconds between balls, lets players shape a session around one drill. Each feed uses a fresh ball from the bag, while the robot’s changing position and timing give the player a more varied sequence to respond to. Topspin, backspin, and lobs up to 26.2 feet (8 meters) over the net add spice, especially for anyone with a shaky overhead.

A responsive session is useful only if getting the equipment onto court isn’t its own workout. Folded down, the A1 has a suitcase-style body, roughly the size of a checked bag, with a pull rod and wheels for the trip from car to court. Its detachable bag holds up to 120 balls, while a racket holder, cup holder, and built-in storage bring more of the practice kit into one unit. At 52.5 pounds (23.8 kg) without the battery, the A1 still takes some planning to load into a car. The suitcase-style layout makes the rest of the journey more manageable.

The removable battery serves the same practical purpose, rated by AceiiLab for up to eight hours of static feeding or two hours of dynamic training from its 36V 7Ah pack. Two hours of moving rallies will tire out most players well before the robot. A charged spare offers a straightforward way to stretch a session into a full weekend of drills. The A1 also works on hard, clay, and grass courts, so it adapts to whatever surface your local club happens to have. Together, the folding body, storage, and swappable power source address the parts of ownership that sit between the product photo and the first ball.

The A1 uses the AceiiLab app on iPhone and Android for training controls, including preset drills, custom sessions, and more competitive Challenge and Ranking modes. Apple Watch support adds wrist-based control, while gestures offer a way to start or pause practice without walking back to the machine. That keeps the player in position and spares a lot of trips across the court, which nobody counts as cardio anyway. candidates.title: A one-liter desktop that runs big AI models on your desk
candidates.full_text:
One liter of chassis holds the whole machine. Gigabyte’s AI TOP AERO runs Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X Superchip, pairing a 20-core Grace CPU with a Blackwell RTX GPU and up to 128GB of unified memory, and it does the work on your desk instead of in a cloud region you will never visit. It is a desktop in the literal sense, too: no battery, no hinge, no screen of its own, just the box and the work.

Gigabyte calls the Aero a Personal AI Studio, and the positioning is specific: local AI development, content creation, and gaming on one Windows 11 machine.

Models load locally, data stays on local storage, and inference runs a few feet from your chair.

Gigabyte AI TOP AERO NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip · Up to 128GB of LPDDR5X unified memory · One-liter chassis Price: TBD Where to buy: More details at Gigabyte

The N1X Superchip integrates the 20-core Nvidia Grace CPU and the Blackwell RTX GPU on a single piece of silicon. Nvidia’s desktop spec for the platform counts 6,144 GPU cores, a 140W thermal envelope, and up to one petaflop of FP4 AI performance, with support for models up to 120 billion parameters and context windows up to one million tokens.

RTX Spark already powers a wave of laptops and desktops, including the machines in our RTX Spark buyer’s guide . Those systems chase thin-and-light designs. The Aero stays plugged in on a desk, trades the battery for a fixed power budget, and spends that budget on sustained loads instead.

The Aero also joins Gigabyte’s existing AI TOP lineup, which already runs from the compact AI TOP ATOM to larger desktop systems.

It is the first of the family built on RTX Spark and Windows, and that puts it in front of a wider audience: individual developers and creators working at home, not only teams with a training budget.

Unified memory is the spec that shapes this machine. CPU and GPU draw from the same pool of LPDDR5X, up to 128GB, so a model loads once and both processors work on it in place. Nothing gets copied across a bus, and nothing gets split apart to squeeze into a graphics card’s separate memory.

Scale is where that pool earns its keep. Models in the 120B class need far more room than a desktop graphics card carries, and the Aero’s ceiling is the platform’s ceiling: the full 128GB, available to the GPU as working space for inference, fine-tuning, and testing.

It also changes iteration speed. A test that waits in a cloud queue runs here the moment you ask for it, and a failed experiment costs minutes at your own desk instead of time on somebody else’s hardware.

Storage runs up to a 4TB PCIe Gen 5 SSD, fast local room for model weights, datasets, and project files. A 10GbE Ethernet port moves those files across a wired network, and Wi-Fi 7 covers the wireless side.

Everything else on the spec sheet supports that memory pool.

Every wired connection sits on the back panel: the power button, DC input, four USB Type-C ports, an HDMI port, and the 10GbE jack. The flanks stay clean, down to a Kensington lock slot on the side, and the front face is all grille.

Gigabyte designed the cooling for sustained work. Inference runs, renders, and generation jobs hold a system at full load for hours, and a one-liter chassis has very little air to work with. The vented panels front and back are the visible half of that thermal design.

Gigabyte publishes no acoustic figures for the Aero, so how loud a liter of cooling gets under load stays an open question.

Developers build, prototype, and fine-tune on it directly, and Nvidia’s Nemotron models give them open models ready for local inference and agentic work. LM Studio and Ollama round out the day-to-day tools for loading a model and testing what it does.

Nvidia PAIR, the Personal AI Router, extends the Aero across a home or studio network, distributing inference tasks to available devices nearby. Long-running agents can sit on the machine around the clock, working against your own files while your main workstation stays free.

Creators get their own lane. ComfyUI builds generative workflows, Nvidia Broadcast sharpens audio and video for recordings and calls, and RTX Video improves video processing and playback quality inside production work.

The Blackwell GPU supports DLSS 5 in compatible games, bringing neural rendering with more detailed lighting and materials to supported titles. Development in the morning, a render queue in the afternoon, a game at night: the Aero is built to stay the only box on the desk through all three.

candidates.title: SlashVibe Gives AI Work a Dedicated Screen and a Detachable Voice Controller
candidates.full_text:
AI tools can help draft a proposal, gather references, and tackle the little jobs that eat into your day. Keeping track of all that activity, however, can become a job of its own. SlashVibe gives those tasks a dedicated spot beside your computer, pairing a small display with a detachable voice controller so checking progress doesn’t always mean opening another conversation.

SlashVibe takes a familiar shape, with a hinged, 3.96-inch LCD above a compact base. There’s no tiny keyboard demanding that you relearn typing with your thumbs. Instead, three action keys and a two-axis joystick handle the shorter interactions. Your computer remains the place for full documents and detailed edits, while SlashVibe is designed around checking, selecting, and responding.

Designers: Changliang Liu, Yitian Wu, Shijun Xu (dooo design)

Take that client proposal, for example. Gathering references and preparing a first draft are related jobs, but they’re still separate pieces of work. Instead, SlashVibe organizes supporting AI tasks under the responsibility they belong to. That gives the screen a purpose beyond showing a collection of busy agents, keeping the project you’re responsible for connected to the work you’ve handed off.

As those agents work, the display shows which sessions are running, finished, or waiting for you. Selecting one can bring its associated window to the front on your computer, while supported permission requests can be handled directly on SlashVibe. The small screen helps you find the thing that needs attention, rather than pretending it should contain your entire working day.

When the draft needs a different emphasis, the next instruction can be spoken instead of typed. Built-in dictation turns that explanation into editable text, with cleanup and formatting designed to make it easier to read. Separate Send and Cancel controls keep speaking and submitting from becoming the same action. After all, thinking out loud shouldn’t have to mean sending every unfinished thought.

The detachable controller makes that voice interaction more interesting than another microphone sitting on a desk. You can bring it closer to speak softly or lean back while composing an instruction, leaving the display where it’s easiest to see. It connects wirelessly to the display, which stays linked to the computer through USB-C. Viewing and speaking don’t have to happen in the same spot.

That split also gives the materials different roles. Sandblasted, anodized aluminum forms the display housing, base, and action keycaps, while the controller uses a plastic housing with soft-touch upper surfaces. Kailh ultra-low-profile mechanical switches sit beneath the keys. Those raised controls give the interface physical landmarks, a deliberate change from another layer of tiny icons competing for attention across your computer screen.

A meeting adds another layer to the same project. Physical recording controls, live notes, and contextual prompts extend SlashVibe beyond supervising agents. You could catch up on a missed point or find a follow-up question without turning your attention to an entirely different window. The joystick provides a way to move through those prompts while the conversation continues.

Afterward, action items become to-dos, with related work available to delegate to AI and full meeting notes available on the computer. A request for another comparison can become the next supporting task for the proposal. SlashVibe’s companion app supports macOS and Windows, and the company lists more than 20 compatible AI agents and tools, including Claude Code and Cursor. The proposal remains the thread connecting those separate sessions and decisions.

The software development kit (SDK) would let developers create dashboards or connect additional agents. A project-specific display could keep the proposal’s supporting work visible while the document itself stays open on the main screen. When another change comes to mind, the controller is already beside the keyboard. A spoken instruction can handle the adjustment while the larger screen stays devoted to the document.
